title: Why Tiny Daily Habits Beat MOTIVATION
title_alternatives: The Science of Getting 1% BETTER Every Day
Why Discipline Is Easier Than You THINK
It Takes 66 Days, Not 21: The Truth About HABITS
Disciplined People Don't Use More WILLPOWER
Small Habits, Big Change: What Science ACTUALLY Says
description:
It doesn't take 21 days to build a habit. In one study it took about 66 on average, and for some people around eight months. Why tiny daily steps beat motivation, why the willpower battery story fell apart in 23 labs, and how disciplined people really win.

This video is psychology for education, not medical or professional advice.

- Galla & Duckworth (2015). More than resisting temptation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
- Amabile & Kramer (2011). The Progress Principle.
- Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement.

scenes.narration: From two hundred thirty-eight people at work.

scenes.narration: On their best days, one thing showed up again and again.

scenes.narration: Not big promotions. Not huge breakthroughs.

scenes.narration: Simply making progress on meaningful work, even small progress.

scenes.narration: Think about your own best day this month.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character smiles, remembering finishing a small task at his desk.

scenes.narration: Small events made up nearly two thirds of what people reported.

scenes.fact_source: Amabile & Kramer (2011). The Progress Principle. Harvard Business Review Press (about 12,000 diary entries from 238 people)

scenes.narration: Usually it's not something huge. It's moving forward.

scenes.narration: Even small steps forward lifted people's mood and motivation.

scenes.narration: Small progress makes you feel good. Feeling good keeps you going.

scenes.narration: Most of the events that mattered were small ones.

scenes.narration: Keeping a simple daily record helped the researchers spot these wins.

scenes.narration: So track tiny wins. A tick on a calendar is enough.

scenes.narration: So, how do you actually improve a little every day?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands at his window at sunrise, coffee in hand, thinking.

scenes.narration: Start smaller than feels useful.

scenes.fact_source: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts & Wardle (2010). How are habits formed: modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology 40, 998-1009

scenes.narration: And make it easy to start.

scenes.narration: Disciplined people in the studies relied on easy routines, not on struggle.

scenes.fact_source: Galla & Duckworth (2015). More than resisting temptation: beneficial habits mediate the relationship between self-control and positive life outcomes. JPSP 109, 508-525

scenes.narration: Expect around two months, not three weeks.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character pins a calendar with two months highlighted, nodding calmly.

scenes.narration: Don't trust a willpower battery. Change your surroundings.

scenes.narration: Miss a day? Come back tomorrow.

scenes.narration: And count every tiny win.
